metadata.note: The Lehigh Valley's Hazleton Branch -- the line that outlived the rest of the railroad's passenger service. The branch left the main line at Penn Haven Junction, north of Jim Thorpe, and climbed west out of the Lehigh Gorge through Weatherly to Hazleton, in the heart of the anthracite country; Weatherly became a junction town when the Hazleton Railroad built down from its namesake to meet the Beaver Meadow road, which the Lehigh Valley acquired in 1864. Branch passenger trains ran east to a terminus at Lehighton rather than into the gorge, so the route drawn here is the Lehighton-Hazleton passenger working. When the Lehigh Valley ended all main-line passenger service on 4 February 1961 with the last Maple Leaf and John Wilkes, the Budd Rail Diesel Cars on this branch kept running for another four days: the very last Lehigh Valley passenger train ran on 8 February 1961.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehighton_station (Lehighton was the eastern terminus for Hazleton Branch passenger trains, although the branch diverged at Penn Haven Junction, north of Jim Thorpe; branch service ended February 8 1961, four days after main line service concluded on February 4 1961)

https://www.trains.com/ctr/railroads/fallen-flags/lehigh-valley-railroad-remembered/ and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehigh_Valley_Railroad (Budd Rail Diesel Car service continued on the Lehighton-Hazleton branch for four days after the main line ceased; all main-line passenger service ended February 4 1961 with the Maple Leaf and the John Wilkes; the Beaver Meadow Railroad was acquired in 1864)

https://www.csxthsociety.org/railfanning/nsformerlehighvalleyhazletonarea20170712n13.html (Weatherly is at milepost 4.3 on the branch; the now-abandoned Quakake Branch entered at Black Creek Junction from Delano; the Hazleton Railroad built down from its namesake to connect with the Beaver Meadows road and Weatherly became a junction town)
geometry_sources: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap end to end -- 26.54 mi Lehighton to Hazleton, with NO straight-line legs and no bridged gaps. Routed through Lehighton, Jim Thorpe, Penn Haven Junction, Weatherly and Hazleton; every station matched within 0.9 km. The Jim Thorpe-Penn Haven leg runs 1.85x its straight-line distance, which is not an error -- that is the Lehigh Gorge, where the line follows the river's meanders. Simplified with Douglas-Peucker at 20 m. NOTE the Lehighton-Penn Haven Junction portion runs over the LV main line, which is also drawn in lehigh_valley_railroad.geojson, so the two overlap there; that is deliberate, because Lehighton was the passenger terminus for branch trains.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: The date passenger service BEGAN on this branch is not sourced. 1864, the Lehigh Valley's acquisition of the Beaver Meadow Railroad, is used as the start because it is the earliest firmly dated LV connection here -- it is NOT a documented first passenger train, and the branch's component railroads predate it. No route mileage was found for the branch, so the 26.9 mi measured here has nothing to check it against; the one milepost that is sourced, Weatherly at 4.3 from Penn Haven Junction, is consistent with this trace. Headways are estimates; the date the branch converted to Budd RDC operation is not sourced.
metadata.related: See lehigh_valley_railroad.geojson for the main line.
metadata.labelling: 2026-08-24: every feature in this file carries 'Lehigh Valley Railroad' at the start of its `line` field, which is what app.js shows in the hover tooltip, so LV routes are identifiable on the map without opening the data. Predecessor companies that were independent at the time are labelled '<Company> (Lehigh Valley predecessor)' rather than being relabelled as LV, because they were not yet Lehigh Valley in the years those features cover.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

segments.note: The Lehigh Valley acquired the Beaver Meadow Railroad in 1864; the Hazleton Railroad had built down from Hazleton to meet it, making Weatherly a junction town. CAVEAT: 1864 is the LV acquisition, not a documented first passenger train on this branch -- see not_yet_sourced. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

segments.note: Branch passenger trains ran Lehighton to Hazleton, leaving the main line at Penn Haven Junction and passing Weatherly at milepost 4.3 and Black Creek Junction, where the Quakake Branch came in from Delano. In its last years the service was worked by Budd Rail Diesel Cars -- and it outlasted the rest of the railroad: when the Maple Leaf and the John Wilkes ended Lehigh Valley main-line passenger service on 4 February 1961, these RDCs ran on until 8 February 1961, the last Lehigh Valley passenger train of all. Frequency estimated, unsourced.
